title: Belief Engine: Making Agent Stance Auditable in LLM Deliberation
claim: A modular pipeline converts incoming text into scored evidence, stores it in memory, and computes an interpretable stance that conditions the response.
layout: 5 stage columns inside a frame, left-to-right, with input/output row below
description: A large rounded blue frame titled "Belief Engine" holds five gray-bordered columns: Extract arguments, Judge evidence, Update memory, Update stance, and Compose response. The first column shows a document icon that yields n_t claims, drawn as green plus and orange minus bars. The second scores claims with strength bars and compares new claims against existing ones, marked with a check or a cross. The third shows a purple Initial seeds box feeding a record card (claim, polarity, source, strength, active flag), then Active z=1 and Archived z=0. The fourth has gauge icons for Uptake u and Anchoring a feeding a Σ log-odds box. The fifth stacks Stance S_t, Memory R_t and Dialogue h_t into an LLM. Below, black boxes for Incoming message and Response y_t sit on either side of a BE agent robot box. Solid blue arrows show the main flow, dashed purple and teal arrows show seeding and retrieval. The eye goes first to the blue Belief Engine frame and the left-to-right stage columns.
caption: Belief Engine architecture. Incoming messages are converted into scored claims and consolidated in structured memory, retaining the stronger of similar claims with the same polarity. In the illustrated active-record mode, only active evidence contributes to stance: uptake u weights later-message evidence, while anchoring a weights initial seed evidence. Weighted contributions are summed in log-odds space and mapped to stance St ∈[−1, 1], from opposition to support. The LLM uses this externally computed stance, retrieved memory, and recent dialogue to generate its reply. Solid blue arrows show per-turn processing; dashed purple and teal arrows show seed initialization and memory retrieval, respectively. Bars and the stance marker are schematic.
abstract: LLM-based AI agents are increasingly used to simulate deliberative social interactions, including negotiation, conflict resolution, and multi-turn opinion exchanges. Simulating human-like opinion change calls for agents that balance existing beliefs with openness to new evidence, while making their responses to that evidence traceable. Current systems often make this difficult: agents may drift from assigned roles, echo an interaction partner, keep a stance despite contrary evidence, or appear to change because the prompt or retrieved context has changed. We introduce the Belief Engine (BE), a framework that uses "belief" in a Bayesian modelling sense, as a maintained evidential state over a proposition that is exposed as a scalar stance. BE extracts structured evidence, stores argument records, and updates the belief state through a Bayesian-inspired stance update in log-odds space with two interpretable controls: evidence uptake u and prior anchoring a. Across multiple LLM models, sweeps of u and a demonstrate stable control over stance dynamics. Higher uptake makes agents more responsive to new evidence, while stronger anchoring preserves the initial stance. On DEBATE, a human deliberation dataset with pre/post opinions, BE is most accurate when participants move in the direction of extracted evidence, showing its strength in evidence-following deliberative contexts. When all participants are evaluated together, gains are more modest because many people remain stable or move for reasons not captured by the extracted evidence stream. BE provides a configurable and auditable belief-update layer for evidence-grounded deliberation, in which LLM agents can be configured as open-minded, anchored, or evidence-sensitive, while their stance trajectories and memory can be audited, compared, and calibrated against human opinion change.
